section.content: 本公开描述了与智能评估器有关的系统、方法和设备。一种设备可解码来自服务消费者的对于创建专门用于机器学习(ML)实体测试的第一被管理对象实例(MOI)的请求。该设备可编码对服务消费者的响应，其中该响应包括对是否接受对MOI创建的请求的指示。该设备可在接受请求时发起ML实体测试。该设备可在ML实体测试完成后针对ML实体测试报告创建第二MOI。该设备可针对服务消费者编码关于此第二MOI的创建的通知。

The present disclosure describes systems, methods, and devices related to intelligent evaluators. A device may decode a request from a service consumer to create a first Managed Object Instance (MOI) specific to a Machine Learning (ML) entity test. The device may encode a response to the service consumer, wherein the response includes an indication of whether to accept the request for MOI creation. The device may initiate ML entity testing upon accepting the request. The device may create a second MOI for the ML entity test report after ML entity testing is completed. The device may encode a notification for the service consumer regarding creation of this second MOI.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning entity testingCross reference to related applications

The application claims the benefit of U.S. provisional application No. 63/393,572, filed on 7/29 at 2022, the disclosure of which is incorporated herein by reference as if fully set forth.

Technical Field

The present disclosure relates generally to systems and methods for wireless communications, and more particularly to artificial intelligence (ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, AI) and machine learning (MACHINE LEARNING, ML) entity testing.

Background

AI and ML entities require accurate testing to ensure optimal performance. There is a need for a system that simplifies test requests, initiates, prepares and synthesizes reports as a reliable framework for evaluating AI and ML entities.

Detailed Description

The following description and the drawings sufficiently illustrate specific embodiments to enable those skilled in the art to practice them. Other embodiments may incorporate structural, logical, electrical, process, algorithm, and other changes. Portions and features of some embodiments may be included in, or substituted for, those of others. The embodiments recited in the claims encompass all available equivalents of those claims.

After the AI/ML entity is trained, verification is performed to ensure that the training process is successfully completed. However, even if verification is successful during development, it is necessary to test and check whether the AI/ML entity is working properly in a particular runtime context (context) or using a particular test data set. The testing may involve interaction with a third party (other than the developer of the AI/ML training function), for example, the operator may use AI/ML training functions or third party systems/functions that may rely on results calculated by AI/ML entities to perform the testing.

After the AI/ML entity training is completed, the AI/ML entity is provided to the consumer(s) via an AI/ML training report when the trained AI/ML entity's performance on both training data and verification data is expected. Prior to applying the AI/ML entity to the target inference function or the AI/ML-enabled function, the AI/ML training MnS producer may need to allow the consumer to evaluate the performance of the AI/ML entity via an AI/ML test process using test data provided by the consumer. The test data has the same pattern as the input part of the training data.

For these reasons, the deployment of AI/ML testing and its control needs to be standardized to enable multi-vendor interactions between different systems. If the test performance is unacceptable or does not meet the predefined requirements, the consumer may request that the AI/ML training producer retrain the AI/ML entity with specific training data and/or performance requirements.

Example embodiments of the present disclosure relate to systems, methods, and apparatus for solutions for AI/ML entity testing of 5G systems (5G systems, 5 gs). Note that in this disclosure, the term "AI/ML" may be used interchangeably with "ML". An AI/ML entity is an ML model or an entity containing an ML model and its associated metadata.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may be conceptualized as an entity similar to a machine learning model. For example, similar to the structure and function of various machine learning models, this entity encompasses complex mathematical formulas representing the core model. However, the entity may also encapsulate additional components that enable efficient management and operation of the model. Thus, while the main aspect of the entity reflects a machine learning model, it also contains other elements that provide an additional layer of manageability to the system.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may operate through multiple phases to enable AI and machine learning to function in a true manner. For example, these phases may encompass a training phase, a verification phase, a testing phase, a simulation phase, a deployment phase, and an reasoning phase. These phases may allow the system to run the model in a simulated real environment, gradually deploying the entity to the target skeleton, and then activating the model to reason in the setup. In addition, the performance of the model is continuously monitored during all of these phases, which together form a comprehensive operational workflow. The goal is to make each operational phase controllable, manageable, monitorable and evaluable, thereby ensuring accountability of the system.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may focus primarily on managing the testing phase of the workflow. This stage includes feeding the model with test data, running an algorithm of the model to generate an inference output, and calculating a performance score based on the test data and the results. Two important use cases are considered here. First, a consumer may request that a particular model be tested using its own test data. The system then evaluates the model and returns the calculated performance score or provides the original inferential output so that the consumer can calculate the performance by itself. The second use case may involve the producer of the system initiating the test independently (possibly based on specific criteria) and then sharing the test results with the consumer.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may incorporate specific control measures, especially when the AI is applied in industries such as telecommunications, where minor errors may lead to significant problems. Historically, each new feature, update or upgrade had to be manually tested by an operator prior to deployment, which is a tedious and time-consuming task. However, with AI, the entire workflow from training to reasoning can be automated, making it more frequent and efficient. Even so, the system ensures that this automated process is always under the control of the operator or consumer, allowing the necessary interventions on demand at any stage.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may employ an information object class (Information Object Class, IOC) to model information or data exchanged between the producer and consumer. This approach allows the information to be handled in a generic way and specific modeling to different use cases. For example, there may be a machine learning test request IOC, representing a test request sent by a consumer, and a network policy IOC, representing a policy for controlling producer initiated tests. In addition, there may be a process IOC that can be controlled by the consumer, and a report IOC that is used by the producer to communicate test results to the consumer. These IOCs are interconnected, process IOCs are associated with requests or policies, and reporting IOCs are linked with processes.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may include a service producer supported by one or more processors. The system may receive a request from a service consumer to create a first managed object instance (managed objected instance, MOI) for ML entity testing. The device may respond to the consumer to indicate whether the MOI creation request is accepted, and may inform the consumer about the creation of the first MOI. The device may prepare for the AI/ML entity test and create a second MOI for the AI/ML entity test procedure in which the consumer is notified. The device may then initiate an AI/ML entity test and may inform the consumer about the progress of the AI/ML test procedure by modifying the second MOI. After the AI/ML entity test is completed, the device may create a third MOI for the AI/ML entity test report and notify the consumer.

In this context, the first MOI may represent an AI/ML entity test request or an AI/ML entity test policy. The first MOI may contain information such as an identifier of the AI/ML entity to be tested, test environment requirements (e.g., expected runtime context), and test data. The first MOI may also contain information such as the identifier or inference type of the AI/ML entity to be tested, the test environment requirements (e.g., expected runtime context), and the test triggers (i.e., conditions that would trigger the test of the AI/ML entity).

The second MOI may contain information such as identifiers of the AI/ML entities being tested, associated AI/ML entity test requests, associated AI/ML entity test policies, test progress, test environment (e.g., test runtime context), and process control (such as cancel, pause, and resume).

The third MOI may contain information such as identifiers of the AI/ML entities being tested, associated AI/ML entity test requests, associated AI/ML entity test procedures, test results indicating success or failure, and inference outputs for each test data instance for success cases, and failure causes for failure cases.

In some embodiments, the service producer may also receive a request from the service consumer to modify the second MOI to control the AI/ML test process, respond to the consumer to indicate whether the MOI modification request is accepted, notify the consumer of the modification of the second MOI, and control the AI/ML test process accordingly in accordance with the modification of the MOI. The modification of the second MOI may be to change an attribute for canceling, suspending, resuming or terminating the AI/ML test process. The creation of any MOI can inform the consumer through a notification, and the modification of the second MOI can also inform the consumer through a notification.

The above description is intended to be illustrative, and not restrictive. Many other examples, configurations, procedures, algorithms, etc. may exist, some of which are described in more detail below. Example embodiments will now be described with reference to the accompanying drawings.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may facilitate AI/ML entity testing of consumer requests.

After receiving the AI/ML training report from the AI/ML training management service (MANAGEMENT SERVICE, mnS) producer regarding the trained AI/ML entity, the consumer can request that the test MnS producer test the AI/ML entity before applying it to the target inference function. In the AI/ML test request, the consumer provides test data having the same pattern as the input portion of the training data.

Any AI/ML entity needs to be tested with specific inputs and features that are appropriate for use cases and for the deployment environment.

AI/ML test the MnS producer performs AI/ML testing using test data provided by the consumer. AI/ML testing is to use test data as an inference input, infer AI/ML entities under test, and generate an inference output for each test dataset instance. AI/ML test MnS producers may be the same as or different from AI/ML training MnS producers. After the AI/ML test is completed, the AI/ML test MnS producer provides a test report to the consumer indicating the success or failure of the AI/ML test. For successful AI/ML testing, the test report contains test results, e.g., an inferred output for each test dataset instance. AI/ML testing MnS producers need to have the required capabilities and provide the required services so that consumers can request tests on specific AI/ML entities or applications or functions containing AI/ML entities and receive the results of the tests. To achieve the desired result, any AI/ML entity needs to be tested with appropriate test data that can reflect the current state of the network in which the AI/ML entity is expected to be deployed. Accordingly, AI/ML test MnS producers need to support the required management services to test AI/ML entities.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may facilitate control of the AI/ML entity test.

Given the test capabilities provided by a given AI/ML test MnS producer, a consumer (e.g., operator) may wish to control and manage the test process capabilities. For example, an operator may wish to define a policy regarding how often a test may be performed on a given AI/ML entity. Accordingly, the 3GPP management system needs to provide the capability to allow configuration of AI/ML entity testing.

The following are some of the potential requirements required for AI/ML testing.

REQ-AI/MLTEST-1AI/ML test MnS producers should have the ability to let authorized consumers request testing of a particular AI/ML entity.

REQ-AI/MLTEST-2AI/ML test MnS producers should have the ability to create test process instances in accordance with the test requests of authorized consumers.

REQ-AI/MLTEST-3AI/ML test MnS producers should have the ability to report the results of a particular instance of the AI/ML test process to authorized consumers, where the results of a successful AI/ML entity test contain the inferential output of each test data instance.

REQ-AI/MLTEST-4AI/ML test MnS producers should have the ability to let authorized consumers (e.g., operators) configure or modify instances of the AI/ML test process.

REQ-AI/MLTEST-5AI/ML test MnS producers should have the ability to test a particular AI/ML entity using specific data specified by the consumer or using data of a location address specified by the consumer or using data having specific characteristics defined by the consumer.

REQ-AI/MLTEST-6AI/ML test MnS producers should have the ability to test a particular AI/ML entity against a specified intended run-time context that the consumer may state.

REQ-AI/MLTEST-8AI/ML test MnS producers should support the ability of authorized consumers to define reporting characteristics that are relevant to a particular instance of an AI/ML test request.

REQ-AI/MLTEST-9AI/ML test MnS producers should support the ability of authorized consumers to manage AI/ML test requests, including suspending, resuming, canceling requests, or adjusting the desired run-time context of the test.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may facilitate a solution for AI/ML entity testing. It should be noted that the names of the attributes or information elements used herein in this disclosure may have different designations.

In one or more embodiments, the intelligent evaluator system may provide a solution based on a network resource model (network resource model, NRM). This solution uses the following example of IOC for the interaction between the AI/ML test MnS producer and consumer to support AI/ML entity testing.

1) The IOC representing the AI/ML entity test request is named MLTestingRequest, for example. The IOC is created on the producer by the AI/ML entity testing MnS consumer and contains the following attributes:

-an identifier of the AI/ML entity to be tested;

Test environment requirements, e.g. expected run-time context;

-test data.

2) IOCs that represent AI/ML entity test policies, for example, are named MLTestingPolicy. The IOC is created on the producer by the AI/ML entity test MnS consumer to control the producer-initiated test, and contains the following attributes:

-an identifier or inference type of AI/ML entity to be tested;

Test environment requirements, e.g. expected run-time context;

Test trigger, i.e. a condition that will trigger the test of the AI/ML entity.

3) IOCs that represent AI/ML entity testing procedures are, for example, named MLTestingProcess. The IOC is created by the AI/ML entity test MnS producer and reported to the consumer, and contains the following attributes:

-an identifier of the AI/ML entity being tested;

-an associated AI/ML entity test request;

-an associated AI/ML entity test policy;

-a test progress; test environments, e.g. test runtime contexts;

control of the process, such as cancel, pause and resume.

4) IOCs representing AI/ML test reports are, for example, named MLTestingReport. The IOC is created by the AI/ML test MnS producer and reported to the consumer, and contains the following attributes:

-an identifier of the AI/ML entity under test;

-an associated AI/ML entity test request;

-an associated AI/ML entity test procedure;

-test results indicating success or failure, and for success cases comprise an inference output for each test data instance, and for failure cases comprise a failure cause.

Fig. 4-6 illustrate various systems, devices, and components that may implement aspects of the disclosed embodiments.

Fig. 4 illustrates an example network architecture 400 in accordance with various embodiments. The network 400 may operate in a manner consistent with the 3GPP technical specifications of LTE or 5G/NR systems. However, the example embodiments are not limited thereto, and the described embodiments may be applied to other networks that benefit from the principles described herein, such as future 3GPP systems, and the like.

The network 400 includes a UE 402, which is any mobile or non-mobile computing device designed to communicate with a RAN 404 via an over-the-air connection. UE 402 is communicatively coupled with RAN 404 through a Uu interface, which may be applicable to both LTE and NR systems. Examples of UEs 402 include, but are not limited to, smart phones, tablet computers, wearable computers, desktop computers, laptop computers, in-vehicle infotainment systems, in-vehicle entertainment systems, dashboards, head-up display (HUD) devices, in-vehicle diagnostic devices, dashboard mobile devices, mobile data terminals, electronic engine management systems, electronic/engine control units, electronic/engine control modules, embedded systems, sensors, microcontrollers, control modules, engine management systems, networking appliances, machine-to-machine (M2M), device-to-device (D2D), machine-to-type communication, MTC) devices, internet of things (Internet of Things, ioT) devices, and so forth. The network 400 may include a plurality of UEs 402 directly coupled to each other via a D2D, proSe, PC and/or Side Link (SL) interface. These UEs 402 may be M2M/D2D/MTC/IoT devices and/or in-vehicle systems that communicate using physical side link channels, such as, but not limited to PSBCH, PSDCH, PSSCH, PSCCH, PSFCH, etc. UE 402 may perform blind decoding attempts for the SL channel/link in accordance with various embodiments herein.

In some embodiments, the UE 402 may also communicate with the AP 406 via an over-the-air (OTA) connection. AP 406 manages WLAN connections that may be used to load transfer some/all network traffic from RAN 404. The connection between the UE 402 and the AP 406 may conform to any IEEE 802.11 protocol. Further, UE 402, RAN 404, and AP 406 may utilize cellular-WLAN aggregation/integration (e.g., LWA/LWIP). cellular-WLAN aggregation may involve the UE 402 being configured by the RAN 404 to utilize both cellular radio resources and WLAN resources.

The RAN 404 includes one or more access network nodes (access network node, AN) 408.AN 408 terminates the air interface(s) for UE 402 by providing access plane protocols including RRC, PDCP, RLC, MAC and PHY/L1 protocols. In this way, the AN 408 enables data/voice connectivity between the CN 420 and the UE 402. The AN 408 may be a macrocell base station, or a low power base station for providing a femtocell, picocell, or other similar cell having a smaller coverage area, smaller user capacity, or higher bandwidth than the macrocell, or some combination of these. In these implementations, the AN 408 is referred to as BS, gNB, RAN node, eNB, ng-eNB, nodeB, RSU, TRxP, or the like.

One example implementation is a "CU/DU splitting" architecture, wherein AN 408 is embodied as a gNB-Central Unit (CU) communicatively coupled with one or more gNB-Distributed Units (DUs), wherein each DU may be communicatively coupled with one or more Radio Units (RUs) (also known as RRHs, RRUs, etc.) (see 3GPP TS 38.401v16.1.0 (2020-03), for example). In some implementations, one or more RUs may be individual RSUs. In some implementations, instead of or in addition to the gNB-CU and gNB-DU, the CU/DU split may include one ng-eNB-CU and one or more ng-eNB-DUs, respectively. AN 408 employed as a CU may be implemented in a separate device or as part of one or more software entities running on a server computer, e.g., as a virtual network including a virtual baseband Unit (Base Band Unit, BBU) or pool of BBUs, cloud RAN (CRAN), radio equipment controller (Radio Equipment Controller, REC), radio cloud center (Radio Cloud Center, RCC), centralized RAN (centralized RAN, C-RAN), virtualized RAN (virtualized RAN, vRAN), etc. (although these terms may refer to different implementation concepts). Any other type of architecture, arrangement, and/or configuration may also be used.

Multiple ANs may be coupled to each other via AN X2 interface (if RAN 404 is AN LTE RAN or AN evolved universal terrestrial radio access network (Evolved Universal Terrestrial Radio Access Network, E-UTRAN) 410) or AN Xn interface (if RAN 404 is a NG-RAN 414). The X2/Xn interface (which may be separated into control/user plane interfaces in some embodiments) may allow the AN to communicate information related to handoff, data/context transfer, mobility, load management, interference coordination, and so on.

The ANs of the RAN 404 may each manage one or more cells, cell groups, component carriers, etc. to provide AN air interface for network access to the UE 402. The UE 402 may be simultaneously connected with multiple cells provided by the same or different ANs 408 of the RAN 404. For example, the UE 402 and the RAN 404 may use carrier aggregation to allow the UE 402 to connect with multiple component carriers, each component carrier corresponding to one Pcell or Scell. In a dual connectivity scenario, the first AN 408 may be a primary node providing AN MCG and the second AN 408 may be a secondary node providing AN SCG. The first/second AN 408 may be any combination of eNB, gNB, ng-enbs, etc.

RAN 404 may provide an air interface over licensed spectrum or unlicensed spectrum. To operate in unlicensed spectrum, a node may use LAA, eLAA and/or feLAA mechanisms based on CA technology and PCell/Scell. Prior to accessing the unlicensed spectrum, the node may perform medium/carrier sense operations based on, for example, listen-before-talk (LBT) protocols.

In a V2X scenario, the UE 402 or AN 408 may be or act as a roadside unit (RSU), which may refer to any traffic infrastructure entity for V2X communications. The RSU may be implemented in or by a suitable AN or a fixed (or relatively fixed) UE. An RSU implemented in or by a UE may be referred to as a "UE-type RSU", an RSU implemented in or by an eNB may be referred to as an "eNB-type RSU", an RSU implemented in or by a gNB may be referred to as a "gNB-type RSU", and so on. In one example, the RSU is a computing device coupled with a roadside-located radio frequency circuit that provides connectivity support to passing vehicle UEs. The RSU may also include internal data storage circuitry to store intersection map geometry, traffic flow statistics, media, and applications/software to sense and control ongoing vehicle and pedestrian traffic flow. The RSU may provide extremely low latency communications required for high speed events such as collision avoidance, traffic alerts, and the like. Additionally or alternatively, the RSU may provide other cellular/WLAN communication services. The components of the RSU may be enclosed in a weather-proof enclosure suitable for outdoor installation, and may include a network interface controller to provide a wired connection (e.g., ethernet) to a traffic flow signal controller or backhaul network.

In some embodiments, the RAN 404 may be an E-UTRAN 410 with one or more enbs 412. The E-UTRAN 410 may provide an LTE air interface (Uu) with 15kHz SCS, CP-OFDM waveform for DL and SC-FDMA waveform for UL, turbo coding for data and TBCC for control, and so on. The LTE air interface may rely on CSI-RS for CSI acquisition and beam management, PDSCH/PDCCH demodulation by means of PDSCH/PDCCH DMRS, and cell search and initial acquisition by means of CRS, channel quality measurements, and channel estimation for coherent demodulation/detection at the UE. The LTE air interface may operate in the frequency band below 6 GHz.

In some embodiments, RAN 404 may be a Next Generation (NG) -RAN 414 having one or more gnbs 416 and/or one or more NG-enbs 418. The gNB 416 connects with the 5G enabled UE 402 using a 5G NR interface. The gNB 416 is connected to the 5GC 440 via a NG interface, which includes an N2 interface or an N3 interface. The NG-eNB 418 is also connected to the 5gc 440 through the NG interface, but may be connected to the UE 402 via the Uu interface. The gNB 416 and the ng-eNB 418 may be connected to each other through an Xn interface.

In some embodiments, the NG interface may be split into two parts, one being a NG user plane (NG-U) interface that carries traffic data between the node of NG-RAN 414 and UPF 448 (e.g., an N3 interface), and the other being a NG control plane (NG-C) interface that is a signaling interface between the node of NG-RAN 414 and AMF 444 (e.g., an N2 interface).

NG-RAN 414 may provide a 5G-NR air interface (also referred to as a Uu interface) with variable SCS, CP-OFDM for DL, CP-OFDM and DFT-s-OFDM for UL, polarity codes, repetition codes, simplex and Reed-Muller codes for control, and LDPC for data. The 5G-NR air interface may rely on CSI-RS, PDSCH/PDCCH DMRS, similar to the LTE air interface. The 5G-NR air interface may not use CRS but may use PBCH DMRS for PBCH demodulation, PTRS for phase tracking of PDSCH, and tracking reference signals for time tracking. The 5G-NR air interface may operate on an FR1 band including a band below 6GHz or an FR2 band including a band from 24.25GHz to 52.6 GHz. The 5G-NR air interface may comprise an SSB, which is a region of the downlink resource grid comprising PSS/SSS/PBCH.

The 5G-NR air interface may utilize BWP for various purposes. For example, BWP may be used for dynamic adaptation of SCS. For example, the UE 402 may be configured with multiple BWP, where each BWP configuration has a different SCS. When the BWP change is indicated to the UE 402, the SCS of the transmission is also changed. Another example of use of BWP relates to power saving. In particular, the UE 402 may be configured with multiple BWPs having different amounts of frequency resources (e.g., PRBs) to support data transmission in different traffic load scenarios. BWP containing a smaller number of PRBs may be used for data transmission with small traffic load while allowing power savings at the UE 402 and in some cases at the gNB 416. BWP comprising a larger number of PRBs may be used for scenarios with higher traffic load.

The RAN 404 is communicatively coupled with a CN 420 that includes network elements and/or Network Functions (NFs) to provide various functions to support data and telecommunications services to clients/subscribers (e.g., the UE 402). The components of CN 420 may be implemented in one physical node or in a separate physical node. In some embodiments, NFV may be utilized to virtualize any or all of the functionality provided by the network elements of CN 420 onto physical computing/storage resources in servers, switches, and the like. The logical instantiation of the CN 420 may be referred to as a network slice, and the logical instantiation of a portion of the CN 420 may be referred to as a network sub-slice.

CN 420 may be an LTE CN 422 (also referred to as evolved packet core (Evolved Packet Core, EPC) 422). EPC 422 may include MME 424, SGW 426, SGSN 428, HSS 430, PGW 432, and PCRF 434, which are coupled to each other through interfaces (or "reference points"), as shown. NF in EPC 422 is briefly described as follows.

MME 424 implements mobility management functions to track the current location of UE 402 to facilitate paging, bearer activation/deactivation, handover, gateway selection, authentication, and so forth.

SGW 426 terminates the S1 interface towards RAN 410 and routes data packets between RAN 410 and EPC 422. S-GW 426 may be a local mobility anchor point for inter-RAN node handover and may also provide anchoring for inter-3 GPP mobility. Other responsibilities may include lawful interception, charging and some policy enforcement.

The SGSN 428 keeps track of the location of the UE 402 and performs security functions and access control. The SGSN 428 also performs EPC inter-node signaling for mobility between different RAT networks, selects PDNs and S-GWs as specified by the MME 424, selects the MME 424 for handover, and so forth. The S3 reference point between MME 424 and SGSN 428 is 3GPP inter-access network mobility enabled user and bearer information exchange in idle/active state.

HSS 430 includes a database for network users including subscription-related information to support the handling of communication sessions by network entities. HSS 430 may provide support for routing/roaming, authentication, authorization, naming/addressing resolution, location compliance, and so on. The S6a reference point between HSS 430 and MME 424 may enable the transfer of subscription and authentication data to authenticate/authorize user access to EPC 420.

PGW 432 may terminate an SGi interface towards a Data Network (DN) 436, which may include an application (app)/content server 438.PGW 432 routes data packets between EPC 422 and data network 436. PGW 432 is communicatively coupled with SGW 426 via an S5 reference point to facilitate user plane tunneling and tunnel management. PGW 432 may also include nodes (e.g., PCEFs) for policy enforcement and charging data collection. Further, the SGi reference point may communicatively couple PGW 432 with the same or different data network 436. PGW 432 may be communicatively coupled with PCRF 434 via a Gx reference point.

PCRF 434 is the policy and charging control element of EPC 422. PCRF 434 is communicatively coupled with application/content server 438 to determine the appropriate QoS and charging parameters for the service flows. The term "SSB" refers to a synchronization signal/physical broadcast channel (synchronization signal/Physical Broadcast Channel, SS/PBCH) block that includes a primary synchronization signal (Primary Syncrhonization Signal, PSS), a secondary synchronization signal (Secondary Syncrhonization Signal, SSs), and a PBCH. The term "primary cell" refers to an MCG cell operating on a primary frequency, wherein the UE either performs an initial connection establishment procedure or initiates a connection re-establishment procedure. The term "primary SCG cell" refers to an SCG cell in which a UE performs random access when performing a reconfiguration procedure with synchronization for DC operation. The term "secondary cell" refers to a cell that provides additional radio resources for a CA-configured UE over a special cell. The term "secondary cell group" refers to a subset of serving cells for a DC configured UE that includes PSCell and zero or more secondary cells. The term "serving cell" refers to a primary cell for a UE in rrc_connected that is not configured with CA/DC, and only one serving cell is composed of the primary cell. The term "serving cell" refers to a set of cells including special cell(s) and all secondary cells for a UE in rrc_connected configured with CA. The term "special cell" refers to a PCell of an MCG or a PSCell of an SCG for DC operation, otherwise the term "special cell" refers to a PCell.

The term "A1 policy" refers to a declarative policy expressed using formal statements that enables non-RT RIC functions in SMO to direct near RT RIC functions, thereby directing the RAN to better achieve RAN intent.

The term "A1 rich information" refers to information utilized by near RT RIC collected or derived at SMO/non-RT RIC from non-network data sources or from the network function itself.

The term "A1 policy based traffic handling processing mode" refers to a mode of operation in which a near RT RIC is configured with A1 policy to use traffic handling actions to ensure a more specific concept of network performance than it ensures in background traffic handling (e.g., for smaller groups of E2 nodes and UEs in the RAN).

The term "background traffic handling processing mode" refers to a mode of operation in which the near RT RIC is configured with O1 to use traffic handling actions to ensure general background network performance, which is widely applicable to E2 nodes and UEs in the RAN.

The term "baseline RAN behavior" refers to the default RAN behavior configured by SMO at the E2 node.

The term "E2" refers to an interface that connects a near RT RIC and one or more O-CU-CPs, one or more O-CU-UPs, one or more O-DUs and one or more O-eNBs.

The term "E2 node" refers to a logical node that terminates an E2 interface. In this version of the specification, the ORAN node terminating the E2 interface is O-CU-CP, O-CU-UP, O-DU, or any combination for NR access, and O-eNB for E-UTRA access.

In the context of an O-RAN system/implementation, the term "intent" refers to a declarative policy for manipulating or directing the behavior of RAN functions that allows the RAN functions to calculate optimal results to achieve a given goal.

The term "O-RAN non-real-time RAN intelligent controller" or "non-RT RIC" refers to a logic function that enables non-real-time control and optimization of RAN elements and resources, AI/ML workflows including model training and updating, and policy-based guidance of applications/features in near RT RIC.

The term "near RT RIC" or "O-RAN near real time RAN intelligent controller" refers to a logic function that enables near real time control and optimization of RAN elements and resources via fine-grained (e.g., UE-based, cell-based) data collection and actions over the E2 interface.

The term "O-RAN central unit" or "O-CU" refers to a logical node hosting RRC, SDAP and PDCP protocols.

The term "O-RAN central unit-control plane" or "O-CU-CP" refers to a logical node that hosts the control plane portion of the RRC and PDCP protocols.

The term "O-RAN central unit-user plane" or "O-CU-UP" refers to the logical node hosting the user plane part of the PDCP protocol and the SDAP protocol.

The term "O-RAN distributed unit" or "O-DU" refers to a logical node hosting RLC/MAC/higher PHY layers based on lower layer functional segmentation.

The term "O-RAN eNB" or "O-eNB" refers to an eNB or a ng-eNB supporting an E2 interface.

The term "O-RAN radio unit" or "O-RU" refers to a logical node that hosts the lower PHY layer and RF processing based on underlying functional partitioning. This is similar to the "TRP" or "RRH" of 3GPP, but is more specific in terms of including low PHY layers (FFT/ift, PRACH extraction).

The term "O1" refers to the interface between the orchestration and management entity (orchestration/NMS) and the O-RAN managed elements for operation and management through which FCAPS management, software management, file management, and other similar functions should be implemented.

The term "RAN UE group" refers to an aggregation of UEs whose packets are also set in the E2 node by the E2 procedure based on the scope of the A1 policy. These groups may then be the targets of E2 CONTROL or POLICY messages.

The term "traffic handling actions" refers to using a mechanism to alter RAN behavior. Such actions include E2 procedures such as CONTROL and POLICY.

The term "traffic handling inner loop" refers to the portion of the traffic handling process triggered by the arrival of periodic TS-related KPMs (key performance measures) from the E2 node, including UE grouping, setting up additional data collection from the RAN, and selecting and performing one or more optimization actions to implement the traffic handling policy.

The term "traffic handling outer loop" refers to the portion of the traffic handling process triggered by the near RT RIC setting or updating the traffic handling aware resource optimization procedure based on information from the A1 policy settings or updates, A1 rich information (ENRICHMENT INFORMATION, EI) and/or the results of the near RT RIC evaluation, including initial configuration (pre-conditions) and related A1 policy injection, TS change trigger conditions.

The term "traffic handling processing mode" refers to a mode of operation in which the RAN or near RT RIC is configured to ensure specific network performance. Such performance includes aspects such as cell load and throughput, and may be applicable differently for different E2 nodes and UEs. Throughout this process, a "flow manipulation action" is used to meet the requirements of this configuration.

The term "traffic steering objective" refers to the expected performance result that is desired to be obtained from the network, which is configured to a near RT RIC by O1.
